newsitem.title: USA: Hurricane Fran pounds U.S. coast, motorist killed.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Fran pounds U.S. coast, motorist killed.

text.p: The outer fringes of Hurricane Fran pounded the Carolina coast with winds of more than 100 mph (160 kmh) on Thursday evening, ripping down power lines, overturning cars and pulling shingles from roofs.

Nuclear power reactors were shut, shops and bridges closed and homes boarded up as people near the border of North and South Carolina awaited the full impact of Fran and its 115 mph (185 kmh) winds, expected before midnight on Thursday.
More than 200,000 residents evacuated low-lying areas and checked into motels, stayed with friends or went to Red Cross shelters to wait out the storm, officials said.
An elderly motorist died on a rain-slicked South Carolina highway when she lost control of her car and crashed into a tree, the state highway patrol said.
By early evening, winds clocked at more than 100 mph (160 kph) had shrieked ashore at Southport, North Carolina, cutting electricity and telephone services in coastal communities.
In Wilmington, North Carolina, emergency officials said they expected the entire city of 60,000 to lose power.
Fran was predicted to cut across the heart of North Carolina, dumping up to 12 inches (30 cm) of rain and flooding rivers swollen from late summer rains.
About 5,000 residents huddled in a dozen Red Cross shelters in Myrtle Beach, a popular seaside resort on the Atlantic coast, local emergency officials said.
Some 7,000 residents and tourists in nearby Wrightsville Beach, Carolina Beach and Kure Beach were evacuated.
At 7 p.m. EDT (2300 GMT), the eye of the hurricane was 70 miles (112 kph) south of Wilmington and moving north-northwest at 16 mph (25 kph).

Wilmington resident Christine Huynh, 32, said she left her mobile home to check into a hotel. "I just didn't want to be in a mobile home during a hurricane. We were in the trailer park during Hurricane Bertha," she said.
Bertha swirled over Wilmington in July, kicking up heavy surf and destroying crops. Wilmington has charming Victorian homes that are the basis of its tourist industry.
South Carolina officials said at least 175,000 residents and tourists were evacuated from Georgetown and Beaufort counties near Myrtle Beach.

Residents of Charleston, a historic port city battered seven years ago by Hurricane Hugo, breathed a sigh of relief as forecasters said Fran's course would put the eye about 100 miles (160 km) to the north. Hugo's 1989 path through the city killed 27 and caused more than $7 billion worth of damage.

Officials predicted that Fran would create a storm surge up to 16 feet (4.8 metres) early on Friday on a stretch of ocean between Myrtle Beach and Wilmington, threatening billions of dollars of beachfront development.
